Charolais cattle, owned by United States interests, are quietly being imported into Canada from areas other than France without going through the elaborate quarantine station established in 1965 in Gross lie, Quebec-

[DOT] (2:40 p.m.)
On April 25, Mr. Speaker, I asked the Minister of Agriculture about this matter but he did not have any information. I am a very co-operative and patient member, I hope. subtopic: MIDDLE EAST-RUSSIAN REQUEST FOR GENERAL ASSEMBLY MEETING

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: MIDDLE EAST-RUSSIAN REQUEST FOR GENERAL ASSEMBLY MEETING
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would direct a question to the Prime Minister. The U.S.S.R. having been prevented or circumvented from effecting a resolution harmful to Israel and the matter now having been put before the secretary general, with a call on the part of the U.S.S.R. for a convening of the general assembly, and the request in this regard having been sent to the various members, what is Canada's reply to this request that the assembly should now be seized of this matter?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. B. Pearson (Prime Minister):
subtopic: MIDDLE EAST-RUSSIAN REQUEST FOR GENERAL ASSEMBLY MEETING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there are still two resolutions before the security council dealing with the matter to which my right hon. friend refers, and in the past it has been the practice not to refer a matter to the general assembly in special session until it had ceased to be dealt with in the security council. The Soviet union have indicated that if these resolutions were proceeded with, the United States resolution in particular, they would veto them. But pending that, as my right hon. friend has stated, they have asked for a special emergency meeting of the general assembly, a request with which 62 members must agree.
We have received a telegram from the secretary general bringing this matter to our

June 15, 1967
Inquiries of the Ministry attention and asking for our agreement or otherwise. The matter is now under consideration. My own feeling, Mr. Speaker, is that we should not object to a meeting of the general assembly because an objection at this time on grounds of procedure would not delay matters very long. Undoubtedly, from the information we have received, they are going to get 62 affirmative votes. Therefore it would be wise not to object to the matter going before the general assembly, without prejudice to the constitutional correctness of the procedure followed on this occasion.

subtopic: MIDDLE EAST-RUSSIAN REQUEST FOR GENERAL ASSEMBLY MEETING
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, might I suggest to the Prime Minister that the answer by Canada should be in the negative, so Canada will make clear to all the world that it will not countenance the kind of attitude toward Israel which the U.S.S.R. has in mind and has shown in the security council in recent days. Would this not be the proper time for Canada to stand up and say we shall not accept this? If 62 other nations agree, well and good, but why should Canada not stand on its own feet?

subtopic: MIDDLE EAST-RUSSIAN REQUEST FOR GENERAL ASSEMBLY MEETING
speechtext: Well, Mr. Speaker, I do not consider that this would be the situation in respect of a request from the Secretary General to express our views as to whether there should or should not be a special general assembly session. I do not believe the refusal to agree to a meeting of the general assembly would have any bearing on the stand we might take at the general assembly. If we have any views on the matter we can express them before the general assembly.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I have kept very carefully, for several months, in order to use it today, a quotation from the London Observer, published in the Vancouver Sun of August 19, 1966.
[English}
Democratic politics is the art of finding sound policies that are also acceptable to the people.
The resolution and the bill that we are about to introduce are of that kind. Those of us who have worked on it, and we worked hard, Mr. Chairman, think that the content of the bill is sound, that it offers the best solution in the circumstances to a most difficult problem. They hope that spontaneously or after reflection the public will agree with them.
For the benefit of those who are not too familiar with the Cape Breton coal problem, Mr. Chairman, may I offer a few basic background elements. The coal industry in the Syclney-Glace Bay district employs some 6,500 people; that is in the mines, in the railways and in the shops. Along with the steel workers they represent one third of the wage earners of the area.
The Dominion Coal Company Limited, a partly owned subsidiary of Dominion Steel and Coal Corporation, that is Dosco, owns and operates No. 12 colliery at New Waterford, No. 21 and No. 26 collieries at Glace Bay.
The Nova Scotia Steel and Coal Company Limited, a wholly owned subsidiary of Dosco, owns the Princess at Sydney Mines, also referred to as Old Sydney, and McBean mine also referred to as Acadia, in the Pictou area. The production of the three collieries of Dominion Coal I have mentioned amounts to 2.6 million tons per year, and they employ 3,790 people on an average. These figures are for 1966. The production of the other group, that is Princess and McBean, is as follows: Princess, about 600,000 tons; McBean, about 200,000 tons, Which is 800,000 tons altogether. Princess employs 1,071 people and McBean 376.
Added to this there is the contribution of the independent operators. There are three of them in Cape Breton and four of them on the mainland. They produce altogether a little less than half a million tons of coal per year. The total production of coal in Nova Scotia in 1966 was 3.8 million tons, and in the Sydney coal field 3.3 million tons. This gives an idea of the importance of that production.
June 15, 1967	COMMONS
What about reserves? Even under the most liberal of geological assessments the coal resources of Nova Scotia comprise no more than 3 per cent of the Canadian coal resources which, as you know, are confined mostly to western Canada. The existing working and structural plant of the seams of the Sydney coal field point to the extension of the coal seams to about 12 miles out to see. Coal is now currently being extracted up to four miles under the sea and at depths approaching 3,000 feet from the sea bottom. I have been down there, as some other members have, and I must say I was surprised to realize that it sometimes takes more than one hour for people to move from the pit head to the face of the mine. Of course the same time is consumed coming back after a day's work.
[DOT] (3:30 p.m.)
Consequently we are faced with increasing problems of transportation, rock pressure and ventilation which bear directly on mining costs and the costs of maintaining safe working conditions. These considerations place a finite limit on the amount of coal which can be recovered, even by using the best tools which current mining technology provide. It should be added, Mr. Chairman, that coal is in competition with other sources of energy in the maritimes and in other parts of Canada and in other parts of the world. We very often read in the daily press and in magazines on the situation in France, Great Britain, Germany and Japan. Coal presents a problem in all of these countries as a result of technological changes. We are not in the nineteenth century any more. Coal today is not the near-exclusive source of energy that it was then. Canada is not the only country in the world with a major coal problem. The situation in regard to coal in the maritimes will be further aggravated if the current offshore exploration program in respect to oil and gas is successful.
A word or two about markets, Mr. Chairman. Fifty-two per cent of the Nova Scotia production is marketed in Ontario and Quebec at very high subsidy cost. May I give some examples. To move coal to Toronto requires a subsidy of about $9, to Noranda about $7.50, to Sudbury about $9.50, to Trois-Rivieres about $8. The remaining 48 per cent, or about 2 million tons, was marketed in the four Atlantic provinces at lesser subsidy costs, the average there being about $6.66. Hon. members know that the maximum federal subsidy is $10.50 in Quebec and Ontario and $8.50 in the Atlantic provinces.
DEBATES	1551
Cope Breton Development Corporation
The current market for Dosco coal in the Atlantic provinces is about 1.1 million tons per year. The thermal power coal market is not expected to grow significantly beyond the 1.5 million tons level in the Atlantic provinces because of the probability, perhaps I should say the certainty, of new power plants being based on oil rather than on coal.
To illustrate the uncompetitive nature of coal, let me say that residual oil is available at Atlantic and St. Lawrence ports at about $2.15 per barrel, which is the equivalent of about $9.10 per ton of coal. Dosco coal at the pithead currently costs about $14 per ton, and with a minimum transportation rate of about $3 per ton the level of subsidy required to make it competitive with oil in the Atlantic provinces and at St. Lawrence ports would be at least $8 per ton.
Feasibility studies have shown that a mine-mouth power plant is not an attractive proposition compared to the shipping of coal to existing generating centres. Some hon. members might disagree with that but this is the best information available to us at this time. The metallurgical coal market of some
500,000	tons to the Sydney steel plant has been largely lost to United States coal due to a high and increasing sulphur content in the Sydney coal, notwithstanding efforts which have been made to purge the sulphur from that coal. Last year 474,000 tons were imported from the United States for the Sydney steel plant and only 120,000 tons from the Sydney coal mines were used by the plant.
The difficulties of coal mining in Cape Breton are thus of long standing, Mr. Chairman. The industry has been investigated by several royal commissions, the last three being in 1946, 1960 and 1966, and also by a collection of committees. During 38 years of subvention payments the Nova Scotia coal industry has received nearly $200 million in subventions. Over half of this has been provided since the public hearings of the 1960 royal commission on coal.
Perhaps it would be well to underline that in 1957-58 the subventions were about $8 million, in 1964-65 $17 million, and that this year they will be $31 million. This figure is a little bloated because it includes some carryover from the previous year. The estimate for next year of $27.4 million gives a better picture of the situation.
The amount of subvention per coal miner represents today over $4,000 annually.

In comparison with production in other countries, for example, strip mining in the United States, I think the figure is four or five times lower than the results achieved in the United States by strip mining. However, I will come back to this because I would not want to give a false impression.
In addition to direct coal subventions, other forms of assistance to Nova Scotia coal mines amount to some $5 million per year. This assistance is provided under the Atlantic Provinces Power Development Act, the Maritime Freight Rates Act, the Canadian Coal Equality Act and the Coal Production Assistance Act.
I have before me the subventions per mine, and if during the course of debate hon. members would like to have them I would be delighted to provide them.
In 1950, following the 1946 royal commission report, Dosco embarked on a $18 million program to rehabilitate the mines and introduce new mechanical coal cutting equipment. This program was financed with the aid of a $7.5 million loan from the federal government under the Coal Production Assistance Act. I might point out, by the way, that the principal and interest payments are now in default by about $5 million.
This financial transfusion, however, was not sufficient. Early in 1965 Dosco informed the government that in order to continue operating it would require large capital grants ranging from $21.5 million to $37.8 million for a second major program of mine rehabilitation.

Subsequently Dosco informed the government that it wished to withdraw from coal mining altogether, and it offered to sell its entire coal mining interests to the government. So the mines will be forced to close unless substantial new capital is provided for rehabilitation and modernization. It is obvious that no commercial organization or financial institution is willing or eager to advance the necessary capital funds.
[DOT] (3:40 p.m.)

The policy followed by the Canadian government has been influenced by several major considerations. One of the first considerations is the limited viability of the Dosco mines.
A factor other than the one I have just stated is the intention of the Dominion Steel and Coal Corporation to get out of its coal mining operations in Nova Scotia.
A third factor is the need for very large capital to modernize and rehabilitate all those mines. A fourth is the lack of a market for Nova Scotia coal without federal subsidies.
I do know that there are markets, as I have often been told, but those markets remain as long as the federal subsidies remain and, moreover, provided those subsidies are increased.
At the present production pace of 3.5 million tons per year, it has been calculated that subsidies would have to reach close to $400 million during the next fifteen years; even then, the basic sources of the problem would not be eliminated. In other words, if we do nothing today, if we simply continue the present policy, fifteen years from now, having spent $300 to $400 million, we will be faced with the very same problem as we have today.

speechtext: As in the past.

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subtopic: PROVISION FOR TAKING OVER COAL UNDERTAKINGS, DEVELOPING INDUSTRY, ETC.
speechtext:
As in the past. I am not here to blame or justify the actions of past governments; I leave that to the conscience of the members of this house. I consider that all the preceding governments meant well, and I am not accusing them of not having done any better.
Of course, we cannot allow this situation to endure. However, nowhere in Canada shall we find one social problem comparable to this one. Here, and I insist upon this because it is the reason for our intervention, here we are faced with an important urban labour force, we are faced with established collectivities
June 15. 1967

which depend almost entirely upon a big industry which is no longer profitable, which cannot survive for more than a few years, by means of substantial subsidies. This is probably the most thorny problem that this country has ever had to meet.
The coal problem in Cape Breton is essentially a social problem. It is because of its concern for the welfare of individuals and collectivities, and not for the welfare of companies, that the government intends to subsidize the regional economy so that it may evolve from a state of subjection to a declining natural resource toward a more wholesome economic situation.
Undoubtedly, extraordinary efforts will be required and that is what we will be asking the house today, to activate the industrial renewal so as to create new jobs in that area.
Since the development of resources is involved, it seems that corrective measures should be left to the province. This opinion was often expressed before me. The answer is that the Canadian government has historically been involved through its subsidies programs which have kept the mines producing long after they would have been forced to close down, and this would have caused considerable economic and social dislocation.
That is why the Canadian government feels somewhat obligated-together with the Nova Scotia government-to provide financial and other assistance as long as the Sydney collieries are operating.

It was in the light of the foregoing circumstances that the government, through the then minister of trade and commerce who is now Minister of Finance, asked Doctor J. R. Donald to investigate the Cape Breton coal situation once again and to recommend a possible solution. Doctor Donald submitted his report and it was tabled in parliament on October 11, 1966. There is much good philosophy in the Donald report. I mention that partly because the hon. member for Qu'Ap-pelle accused me yesterday of lacking philosophy in the presentation of my estimates. There is much good philosophy, as I said, in the Donald report.
Doctor Donald examined the coal industry not in isolation but in relation to the broad economic and social conditions prevailing in that region. His approach was not only economic and financial; it was also humanitarian and social. His recommendations are based on the fundamental premise that even on a heavily subsidized basis the realistic working

Cape Breton Development Corporation life of the Sydney mines can hardly exceed about 15 years, and that the government should use this period to prepare in a positive manner for the cessation of coal mining. This preparation must involve the creation of new foundations for the Cape Breton economy and a new and more attractive economic environment. That is the only way to forestall the economic debacle which would otherwise result from the closure of the mines.
Doctor Donald says that the choice is not one of preserving or not preserving coal mining indefinitely; the choice is one of planning or failing to plan for what is inevitable. The government is indebted to Doctor Donald for his analysis of the Cape Breton coal problem and for his imaginative and enlightened recommendations. I am pleased to see him in the gallery of the house at this time.
The report was criticized at first, mostly, of course, by the miners and also by other people, some of whom said it was not generous enough while others said it was too generous. I have always been comforted when people around me say that I do not move fast enough or others that I move too quickly. I expect that Doctor Donald also likes this position.

Mr. Chairman, I feel that this report will be a landmark in the economic history of Canada. Doctor Donald made many recommendations, but considering the lack of time I will not spell them out. We have agreed to very many of them and they will be found in the legislation and in the agreement that was tabled today.
On December 29, 1966, the government, I repeat, following careful consideration of the Donald report and its recommendations, the receipt of views of interested persons and organizations, and discussions with the government of Nova Scotia, announced in consort with Nova Scotia certain basic points of policy. The Minister of National Health and Welfare and I went down to the area to listen to the views of the people. We have received many views since then, just as other ministers had received many views before. As I say, on December 29 in consort with Nova Scotia we
June 15. 1967
1554	COMMONS
Cape Breton Development Corporation announced certain basic points of policy. May I spell them out.
1.	We agreed that parliament be asked to establish a suitable crown corporation, in which both Canada and Nova Scotia will participate, to acquire, reorganize and manage the coal mining interests of the Dominion Steel and Coal Corporation and simultaneously to help promote and finance the development of industry on the island of Cape Breton.
2.	For these purposes, Canada agreed to make a contribution of $45 million to the crown corporation, for the rehabilitation and operation of the mines about $25 million and for the development of new industry about $20 million.
3.	Nova Scotia agreed to contribute $10 million to the initial economic development fund of the corporation.
4.	In place of the present system of providing subsidies to a private corporation on its individual coal sales, the government agreed to request parliament to provide funds to the crown corporation to enable it to mine and market its coal to the best advantage, that is, to underwrite the annual coal losses of the crown corporation.
5.	Canada agreed to augment the initial industrial development fund of the crown corporation from expected savings in federal subsidies resulting from reductions in the level of coal production.
6.	It was agreed that the crown corporation, in rationalizing the mines, should give full consideration to the need for orderly adjustment, including the implementation of a generous early retirement plan as recommended by Doctor Donald.
7.	In view of the federal government's acceptance of the major financial responsibility for the long-term solution to the coal problem of the Dosco mines in the Sydney area, a problem of national concern, Nova Scotia agreed to accept complete responsibility for the independent coal mines of Nova Scotia. These are the several independent coal mines that I have already referred to.
[DOT] (3:50 p.m.)
8.	Nova Scotia agreed to consult with the crown corporation on coal markets in order to maintain an orderly market for Nova Scotia coal.
9.	Nova Scotia agreed, moreover, to issue no further coal mining permits or leases during the next 15 years unless the application for the coal permit or lease carries the approval of the crown corporation.


10.	The opening of a new mine at Lingan has been a matter of much controversy. In view of the government undertaking of October, 1965 and of Doctor Donald's strong recommendation against it, the government agreed to allocate sufficient money to fulfil its own commitment but to leave to the crown corporation the decision as to how these sums can best be used in the interests of the community.
11.	Canada and Nova Scotia agreed to establish a joint framework which will permit the concentration and co-ordination of all federal and provincial efforts to promote the economic development of Cape Breton island.
There are all sorts of organizations already in existence at the federal and provincial levels. We do not want to duplicate these efforts. There will be a great need for co-ordination between the two levels of government.

The agreement I have tabled today contains provision for co-operation between Ottawa and Halifax in a number of areas which I shall enumerate. They include the form and functions of the Cape Breton Development Corporation and of its two divisions, the coal division and the industrial development division; the responsibility of each government in respect of the corporation; the matter of the annual capital and operating budgets of the two divisions of the corporation; the annual report of the corporation-the corporation will, of course, have to report to both governments; the early provision of a target phaseout timetable for the coal mines; the general means by which the two governments will co-ordinate economic development activities on Cape Breton island; the acceptance by Nova Scotia of responsibility for the independent coal operations; the agreement that no further coal mining permits or leases will be issued for the next 15 years without the approval of the corporation, and so on.
Thus, the two preoccupations of the corporation are the nationalization of the mining operations and the stimulation of industrial development in Cape Breton. Both are of equal importance. Can Cape Breton be stimulated? Can the economic base of Cape Breton be broadened to use the wording of the resolution? My colleague the Minister of National Health and Welfare will, I hope, take part in this debate. He will tell the house about recent developments in Cape Breton and about the federal contribution to these developments. He will tell us about the contribution made by the various departments-transport, public works, industry, manpower-and about the contribution made by the agencies of the government such as the Atlantic Development Board and ARDA. He will tell us about the new industrial park at Point Edward, about the new heavy water plants, about the new B.A. refinery project at Point Tupper.
I have studied these things with him. I have taken part in some of the negotiations and consultations which led to some of these projects, and I must say I am optimistic. Hon. members expect that from me, anyway. But very often in the past we have been told that there is no future for Cape Breton in coal and steel. Present events are demonstrating, I think, that there is a future for Cape Breton, partly out of coal, anyway, and that Cape Breton can be modernized.
I have read a report on the B.A. refinery project for Point Tupper which is of extreme
DEBATES	1555
Cape Breton Development Corporation interest. This project could contribute immensely to the broadening of the economic base of Cape Breton.
The purpose of the forthcoming legislation is to delegate to an autonomous crown agency the responsibility for carrying on this developmental work. I am well aware that problems of the magnitude which face Cape Breton island cannot be solved by governments alone without the full support of the people themselves. Without their help one cannot arrest the social blight which has afflicted their area. That we shall receive their support I have no doubt, for as Mr, Justice Rand wrote at page 50 of his report in 1960:
The people who make up the communities concerned, miners and their families, clergy, professionals, tradesmen, skilled and unskilled workers, are of the ordinary stuff of Canadians and, to general, are outstanding in personal relations, in friendliness and hospitality.
One cannot imagine such a people failing to-respond to this new challenge. I am sure they will take an active part in the rebuilding of the economic basis of their island.

I and I think all other hon. members directly interested in the coal industry in Nova Scotia are willing to expedite the passage of this resolution in order that we may get the bill before the house, at which time we may have further remarks to make. However, when making his arguments on behalf or in favour of Cape Breton whichever way one wants to look at them, the minister returned to another touchy subject, and I think it is time the government told the people of Canada the truth with respect to what is involved in subventions or subsidies paid to support Cape Breton coal mining. I appreciate very much, and I hope I will continue to appreciate, what is being done now for the mining situation in Cape Breton, but it is only right that the committee be given more of the history of what mining has meant to Cape Breton and what future developments to replace mining will mean.
At present in the town of Sydney Mines 38.6 per cent of the actual working force is employed in the coal mines. In the Glace Bay area 38 per ent of the actual working force is employed in coal mines. In the town of New Waterford 56 per cent of the actual working force is employed in coal mines. This gives an over-all average of 44 per cent of the work force employed in the mines. Everybody must understand what that means to the economic base of the area. Without the mines there would be no such towns. They could not possibly exist without the work which the mines provide.
Prior to the 1963 election Liberal candidates in Cape Breton as part of their platform said that a Liberal government would bring about great development, would start a research program and look after sales. But history moves on, and on October 5, 1965 in the city of Halifax, not in the coal mining area, the Minister of National Health and Welfare made a grand promise of $25 million to mechanize and improve mining in Cape Breton. Not only did he promise $25 million but poll workers for the Liberals in all the mining towns had the flat statement in their instruction books that $25 million would be given to the coal industry in order to put new life into it.
History moves on further to 1967 and now, despite assurances given over the last 20 months by the Prime Minister, the Minister of Transport, the Minister of National Health and Welfare, the Minister of Energy, Mines
[Mr. Maclnnis (Cape Breton South) .1

and Resources and the Minister of Industry-you name them, they are all included- that the policy announced on October 5, 1965 would be carried out, we have here what I hope will prove to be the answer to our problems. Unfortunately, however, another problem is developing. Mention of this other problem was made today by the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources, although this resolution does not tie in with it. We all hope that the future new development will have favourable consequences and that it will prove to be what we all hope it will be and give new opportunity to the working force.
I trust that the bill to the resolution will give an assurance to each and every miner that before he is displaced from a colliery he will receive employment elsewhere. The difficulties in this connection will be tremendous, because one cannot just phase out a coal mining operation by taking individuals out of the mine. As many as 300, 400 or 500 new jobs will have to be available for the men taken out of a coal mining operation. There is also the question of training to be considered. The government will have a hard task before it.
I draw some satisfaction from the fact that, following passage of this resolution and the bill which will come before us on Monday, until the new development corporation can get its schemes off the ground the miners will have the protection of this legislation. However, I take strong exception to some remarks made by the minister. Since 1963, when the government took office, its members have been unable to differentiate between subvention and subsidy. Today the minister referred to subsidies and what they would mean. He used the word subsidies and said they mean a total of $4,000 per year to each and every miner employed in the coal industry.
The hon. member for York South questioned this figure and referred to the fact that Doctor Donald used the figure of $3,500. Doctor Donald was the commissioner appointed by the government to look into the matter of subsidies, and that was the figure he used. We have a situation where Doctor Donald says $3,500, one minister says $4,000 and another minister says $7,000, and we keep on hearing these ministers use the word subsidy. Let it be understood by the minister once and
June 15, 1967

for all that it is not only the miners who are covered by the subventions. Without these subvention payments we could not get our coal to market, but the subventions cover any number of C.N.R. employees and the employees of other carriers. The subventions are paid to the carriers; they are not subsidies paid to the coal company itself.
The minister is still shoving the same old argument down our throats with respect to what the government has been doing. With regard to the acquisition of the coal mines from Dominion Coal, I should like to refer in part to the policy statement of the Prime Minister on Cape Breton coal which was released on December 29, 1966. At the bottom of the first page and the top of the second page it reads as follows:

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I suggest that the hon. member for Cape Breton South was right, for two reasons, when he twitted the minister and others for constantly repeating the total amount paid by way of subventions or subsidies. First, subsidies and subventions of one sort or another are not new in the development of the Canadian economy. I have a great deal of sympathy with the miners of Nova Scotia for resenting the implication of the suggestions constantly made that they have been beneficiaries of particularly privileged treatment, when in fact subventions have been made over the years to the western coal producers and support prices have been instituted for other products and resources in our economy.
An economy such as Canada's, stretched over many thousands of miles from one ocean to the other, frequently presents the country with a need to support the production and transportation of a particular product, one instance being to bring cheaper fuel to the markets in central Canada. My friends in Cape Breton, Nova Scotia generally and the other Atlantic provinces refer at times to those in upper Canada as having been greedy throughout the 100 years history of this country. I agree with the hon. member for Cape Breton South in his objection to the constant reference to subsidies. But, second, that is not the problem. The problem, as the minister has stated and as Doctor Donald has stated, and as many other inquiries before Doctor Donald's have established, is the constant, almost total economic deterioration of a whole community, and the fact that the two major industries on which the community of Cape Breton has depended and still depends have been over the years on a toboggan slide downward. For this reason, even though my colleagues and I of course support the belated but useful step taken by the government as

indicated in this resolution, I submit that once again this government and this parliament under the leadership of the Liberal government will take a half step instead of a full step to deal with the community problem of Cape Breton because the resolution deals with only one industry in the area.
The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources referred in glowing terms to the report of Doctor Donald. Undoubtedly it is a very important document, couched in concern for the community and the human problems involved. But his terms of reference, as I remember the statement in his report, were limited to a consideration of the coal industry. So he considered that industry. But the fact is that there is another industry on which Cape Breton's future depends and that industry is also going down. The same corporation is involved. Unemployment is increasing in that industry, in the Sydney plant. Neither this resolution nor the legislation to be based on it deals in any way with the second industry which is the basis of the Cape Breton community, namely, the steel industry. That is my complaint and the complaint of my colleagues about steps now being proposed by the government. I will come back to that in a moment, if I may, Mr. Chairman.
I went to Cape Breton island for the first time about 30 years ago. I do not recall whether I had the privilege of meeting the hon. member for Cape Breton South at that time. He is probably too young. But the thing that has struck me over the 30 years-and the blame for this lies at the door of this and other governments, federal and provincial-is that every time I have gone back to Cape Breton, and I have done so, I suppose, about 20 times in the 30 years, I have found that the same problems existed but they had grown worse every subsequent time I visited there.
Inquiry after inquiry has been held. The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources referred to one of them. I think there have been four of five inquiries. The volumes of the reports and their supplementary data could fill a library. Almost every one of the reports-and over the years I have studied most of them-has emphasized the need of doing something fundamental, even though none of them was quite as extensive and broad as Doctor Donald's and, I would say, Mr. Rand's report of 1960, if my memory serves me right.
For all these years we did nothing as a country or as a province. What has been the result? I think it is important for everyone of us, those of us like myself who do not live in
June 15, 1967

Nova Scotia or Cape Breton, to realize what we as a country have allowed to happen in Cape Breton. It is not the fault of the people in Cape Breton. It is superfluous for me to say, as I am sure every member of this house who has visited that island will agree, that the people of Cape Breton are as industrious and as devoted to Canada and their community as any other people in this country. It is not their fault. It is the direct fault of a corporation, a non-human, indeed inhuman copora-tion that has exploited the coal and other resources of that province.
In the case of the steel plant at Sydney, at the turn, of the century this corporation was given municipal tax incentives by the city. It was given other incentives. Through the years it has received almost $200 million in subventions, subsidies and other assistance and has cared not a fig for the future of the community. It has cared not one iota for the future of the people of Cape Breton island and the communities they have built. It has taken all the largesse throughout these years from the federal, provincial and municipal governments. After these moneys had been paid the corporation closed down mines and is now closing down, bit by bit, the Sydney steel plant.
My social philosophy is well known to members of this house. Perhaps one of the most typical examples of what I am saying is to be found in what Dr. MacKintosh once said. Dr. MacKintosh is a famous Canadian economist. I have his words before me. With respect to the capitalist or free enterprise system he said:
[DOT] (4:40 p.m.)
It draws a very bad mark indeed for its allocation of the penalties of the destructiveness of change.
This is exactly what has happened. The people of Cape Breton have paid the penalty. Dosco and the government have paid no attention to the long-range problem. I should like to cite from a speech by Reverend A. Hogan to the 18th dominion-provincial coal conference on September 16, 1966. He is a well known economist who teaches at St. Francis Xavier and he has been interested in Nova Scotian social and economic matters, particularly those relating to Cape Breton, for a good many years. In addition he is, if I may say so, a social economist instead of one of those economists who claim not to make any
Cape Breton Development Corporation moral judgments. He makes them, and I respect him for it. This is what he says in the speech to which I have referred:
All of us know from common observation and history, as well as a general understanding of the nature of our economic system, that the decline and disappearance of an industry is not a new thing. We especially realize this in regard to the gradual depletion of the economic seams of a non-renewable resource such as coal or any other mineral.
Yet I venture to say that for many of us regardless of age, education or skill, the experience of being caught up in such a ferment of change with all its implications, is an abstract one.
I am trying not to make it abstract for myself and for those who are listening to me.
We've read about such occurrences, heard about them, but rarely if ever have concrete experience with what this type of upheaval means, in social and economic terms.
As have hon. members who represent ridings on Cape Breton island.
At a deeper psychological level we are scarcely aware of the emotional impact in terms of fear, suspicion, despair and even rage that a severe dislocation effects in relationships between individuals and groups at such a time.
This is the kind of problem with which governments, federal and provincial, have been faced for many years. The Reverend Mr. Hogan also says in the same speech, and it is worth putting a few of these quotations on the record, that one of the consequences of the neglect of Cape Breton as a community by the corporation, Dosco, which has been the main corporation in the community, as well as by the provincial and federal governments, has been a constant migration from Cape Breton. This has resulted not only in a loss of population but a loss of that adult population which is productive. Thank you, Mr. Chairman, and I thank the members of the committee. The government talks about building new industry but takes no steps now to ensure that an important industry, which according to many experts could be made economically viable and on which so much of the economy of Cape Breton rests, is not allowed to continue to go down the drain, as is the steel industry in Sydney as a result of deliberate action taken by Dosco.
I said before, Mr. Chairman, that if the minister should say or if anyone should suggest that the corporation it is proposed to establish will be free to assist Dosco to modernize its plant in Sydney and so on, then as far as I am concerned-and I think I speak also for all of my colleagues-I have no confidence whatever in the intentions of this giant corporation which has bled Cape Breton island for decades and has left nothing of value in return. I certainly have no confidence in them knowing that the decisions are not made by Dosco but are made by the large international corporation, Hawker Siddeley, of which Dosco is now a part.
Second, Mr. Chairman, I say to the minister that there is no evidence whatever that any help that Dosco gets to rebuild its plant in Sydney will be used for the purposes that he and I have in common. There is only one way. I would urge the minister, as the members of the C.C.F. party and the New Democratic party have urged govermnents over the past 30 years, to accept that the only way to save the steel industry in Nova Scotia and thus to save the second most important industry in the Cape Breton economy, is to bring the steel industry as well as the coal industry under public ownership through the crown corporation being set up.

Cape Breton Development Corporation
This crown corporation would be able to formulate a plan and would have the opportunity to co-ordinate the two basic industries in Nova Scotia. Even if the coal industry were eventually phased out, I venture to prophesy, though this is dangerous to do particularly for a layman, albeit one who has made some study of the subject, that there will be a coal industry in Nova Scotia for many years to come. The industry will be modernized.
The Prime Minister said in his statement that coal production should be reduced to two million tons. However, even that means a relatively substantial industry for that community and it would take a good many years to achieve that reduction. I am not saying that I agree with the Prime Minister because I honestly do not know. I am prepared to leave the matter to the corporation, which because it is a public corporation will, I hope, act with the welfare of the community at heart rather than act in the heartless way in which Dosco, as could be expected, in fact acted.
I am not saying that I agree with the Prime Minister's estimate of two million tons or with the conclusions of Doctor Donald, though I have every respect for the competence of Doctor Donald and I am not contradicting him. But for the purpose of the present discussion I am saying that it will take many years before this reduction to two million tons per year will take place, and this in itself will retain a pretty substantial coal mining industry in that particular community.
Therefore, I suggest that the corporation ought to be given authority over both steel and coal. I am informed both by those who have studied the subject and from my own reading that it is perfectly possible to produce in Sydney various shapes and sizes of structural steel both for use in the Atlantic provinces and for export, particularly to developing nations. I am also told, and I understand from my reading on the subject, that all of this will require a great deal of modernization of plant as well as the introduction of new equipment. This is something Dosco would not undertake; if they wanted to do it they would have done it before. They did not have to do this at Contrecoeur. No one forced them to go to Contrecoeur. Therefore it is obvious they would not undertake this in Sydney; it can only be undertaken as a result of public ownership.
I want to spend a minute or two on one other subject and I will be through, Mr. Chairman. I am very concerned about the

I hope-I say this with some sense of responsibility-that those companies will not receive any compensation under the circumstances. I emphasize the words "under the circumstances" so that no one will take that sentence out of context and say on political platforms across the country that the hon. member for York South, or the deputy leader of the N.D.P., or David Lewis, however they put it, says that he is in favour of not compensating an industry when the government takes it over, because this would not be true. I am in favour of compensating companies when they deserve compensation, when what the company in question hands over is a going concern.
What is happening in this case, Mr. Chairman? The coal mines are not owned by Dosco or by the subsidiaries of Dosco. They are, of course, crown property and Dosco is supposed to pay royalties for the use of the land. But what assets does the company have? Since only the coal mines are being taken over, this means that this company will be saved the headache of carrying on an industry which has lost money for years. What compensation should a company receive for being relieved of a headache? That is what I should like to know. We would be much more justified in saying to Dosco that it was about time that they paid something out of the huge treasury of Hawker-Siddeley ins-stead of putting their hands in the public treasury to pay their preferred shareholders, or whoever it is, when they are operating a losing proposition.

I am not saying this merely because I am being hard on a company but because one of the subjects raised by the hon. member for Cape Breton South is important. If the minister or the federal government have an extra $1 million or $2 million or $3 million to spare, then, instead of giving it to the company which does not deserve it, they ought to give it to the pensioners of the Dominion Steel and Coal Company.


As the hon. member for Cape Breton South said, if my memory serves me correctly, in 1952 or 1953 this company reduced the gratuity which it paid to its retired employees. The hon. member is really justified in what he says. I am not saying he is justified in his legal arguments with the Minister of National Revenue because those have to do with another subject, but he is justified in characterizing what the company paid not as a pension but as a gratuity. There was no pension plan; not only was it non-contributory but there was no fund. It was entirely unfunded. Whether somebody got the pension depended on the company's will and when the company decided 15 years ago to cut the pension it did so and no one had any recourse; no one could do anything about it. Whether or not there is any spare money, I think that the welfare of the pensioners of the Dominion Steel and Coal Company and of the other coal company ought to have priority. I know that my colleague, the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway, wrote to the Minister of Industry about this pension problem. That minister handed the letter over to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources, and I know that the hon. member for Cape Breton South and others have raised this matter many times.
I say, Mr. Chairman, that the bill ought to give three guarantees, which are as follows: First, that whatever pension is now being paid will be taken over by the new corporation, because as the payment was in the form of a gratuity rather than a pension the new corporation could make that payment disappear in law. I hope that the bill will show that that guarantee is included. Second, that the bill will contain a guarantee that those who are now retired will have their pension increased to a decent level, at least to the level of some years ago before the company reduced it. Third, that the promise of the Prime Minister that Doctor Donald's recommendation for a generous and just retirement plan will be adopted will also be written into the law as a guarantee, because God knows what might happen were the members of the board of directors of the new corporation or the bureaucracy left without some statutory guidance on these points and problems that might arise.
I wish it had been possible-with all my heart I say this-for me as the first spokesman for our party today to say to the minister, "You have taken a useful and important step and I have no criticism of it in general terms, whatever criticism we might have

when we see the details." I cannot say that. To do a real job for the Cape Breton community and to assure all the people of that community that a new dawn has really risen and that they can look forward to a future of progress, which might even attract those young people who have left the community back to it, the government in this resolution and in the legislation ought to have included steel as well as coal. Their failure to do that proves to me once again for the umpteenth time that from the government, with its social and economic concept and conscience, we can at best expect a half step taken under the duress of desperation but never a full step.
That is why I cannot extend the kind of heartfelt thanks that I should have liked to extend with respect to the resolution before us and the promised legislation. The step could be important. Whether it will be will depend on what the government does in the future with the steel industry and the coal industry and will depend particularly on the imaginativeness with which new industry is brought into the community and how community needs are geared to the reception of new industry.

Finally, I wish briefly to bring up the subject of the compensation to be paid to the company which now owns the operations to be taken over by the crown corporation. We in this party do not believe that the federal treasury has any inherent responsibility even in this situation to compensate shareholders for the loss of an asset which apparently has no market value. I believe it may be a bad precedent for the government to agree to pay any arbitrary amount as compensation for so-called assets which are really no assets at all. These undertakings have exhausted their value as viable economic units. I say it would be a bad precedent to pay compensation because it would establish that in one case at least the government had taken over a dying industry, on the grounds that a social problem was involved, to the benefit of shareholders who were not part of that social problem. We can look across Canada at prosperous areas as well as depressed areas and find examples of businesses which have failed causing hardship to their employees and to the surrounding communities, and we are apprehensive about giving our approval to any substantial payment being made for an alleged asset which really has no value.
It has been pointed out by several hon. members that the marketable value of the Dosco assets is nil except, perhaps, for some salvage. We do not believe it is the proper function of the federal government to bail out the people involved in a corporation, at the end of an industry's life, when those people are not part of the social problem with which we are trying to deal. What matters here is the welfare of the people of the communities on Cape Breton island, not the situation of those either in Canada or abroad who may happen to own shares in the corporation. So I hope the government does not intend to raid the federal treasury to pay people who, as I

As I say, I made this statement a few hours after the report was tabled and I had only time just to skim through it. This is what I said:
Since I have not had an opportunity to thoroughly digest all of the long-awaited Donald report, I feel that while it certainly paints a black future for Cape Breton in many ways, it also has some good points.
The recommendation for the Cape Breton Development Corporation looks excellent on paper; how it will work out in actual practice is another matter. If this corporation were established, it would have to bring new employment to our island post haste and provide displaced miners with new jobs with a pay equivalent to what they are already earning or more, and not subject them to a long period of unemployment.
We are all aware of the efforts made by Industrial Estates Limited over the years to bring industry into our area, and while they have made excellent progress we have seen that it requires a tremendous expenditure to provide even a few jobs. Further to that, we have been faced with the loss of 650-700 jobs at the Point Edward naval base through the actions of the present government, and within the next year or so we are going to see another 600 to 700 men displaced at the North Sydney ferry terminal, again through the present government's action. So, I would think that this, along with the recommendations of Dr. Donald, would mean that such a corporation would have to act and act very quickly.
The member for Inverness-Richmond on October 5th, 1965, made a definite commitment on behalf of the government that a new mine would be opened in the Lingan area, plus several million dollars of new capital for rehabilitation and modernization of existing mines. Strangely enough, Mr. MacEachen's policy announcement came only several weeks prior to the last federal election. He, along with the Prime Minister and Minister of Transport, have reiterated this commitment on a number of occasions since. Surely they are not going to back down on such a commitment at this time. Mr. Chairman, let me say at the outset that I support this resolution wholeheartedly. I look forward to the bill and to the results of that bill possibly with more anticipation than the minister seems to possess. What I have to say is not on the resolution or the contents of the proposed bill, but about the mood that prevails in this house. It seems to me, having listened to the debate here that there is something lacking. Optimism is lacking. I have attended wakes at which a greater air of optimism was noticeable than during the introduction of this measure.
Consider what was said. The minister pointed out that in reality what this resolution anticipated was a development corporation which, over a period of time, will cost us about $155 million. The hon. gentlemen from Cape Breton North and South pointed out the social benefits that would flow from this measure. There was some argument over whether or not a subsidy was involved. However, no one has yet said what will be the results of this legislation. What do we expect
June 15, 1967

the benefits of this corporation will be? Now, surely if that attitude prevails at a time when young people, the active people of this country are going forward with great strides and undertaking great ventures, we will not attract them.
Here, we have a development corporation. The minister, who has a keen sense of the meaning of words, should tell me what we mean by a "corporation". Do we mean a group of individuals incorporating themselves into a body for the purpose of undertaking something, something that would bring beneficial results to Canada? Here we seem to have a development corporation-of course, I do not believe it is going to turn out this way-which is going to die, judging by the attitude that prevails here.
Comments were made from the other side that we should make sure we do not use worn out politicians on this board. Well, do you expect you are going to get an active group of people together to run this corpration, if it appears to have no future? This is my argument, and I am not referring to the resolution or the bill, which seem to be good. I should like to see some measure of confidence exhibited, some anticipation of beneficial results, rather than just the impression that the corporation will spend money without any idea aboxit how we are going to make this corporation worth while.
I want to say a few words about the minister's remarks, as well as the remarks of other hon. gentlemen, about how this corporation is going to entice industry into Cape Breton. I think we should be rather pragmatic about this. Industry will not go to an area unless it foresees a future for itself. Surely, as a short term prospect, it will go to an area if it is given tax concessions. Essentially, however, industrial expansion requires that some advantage be given to industry. You must give industry something more than it gets elsewhere. You may give cheap electrical power, and you will entice industry. If you give raw materials not found elsewhere, you will entice industry. A fluid labour market, specialized skills, transportation facilities to markets- these things will entice industry.
What are you going to give industry in Cape Breton? Are you going to give cheap power? Are you going to give proximity to markets or a fluid labour supply? What will you give? The minister has not explained in what way industry will be convinced to go into Cape Breton on a long term basis. I suggest that we have the answer, but it takes some daring and it takes some confidence. Let me 27053-101
Cape Breton Development Corporation point out to the minister the present situation in connection with the heavy steel industry. The ore goes from Labrador and by boat through the great lakes to Chicago. Coal is brought in from Pittsburgh and the southern United States. Steel is made and then the finished product is brought back down the St. Lawrence to the New York market, the Montreal market and the world market.
[DOT] (8:10 p.m.)
Let us consider that ore, a very heavy commodity, is brought all that distance, six times the distance between Sept lies and Cape Breton. In spite of this, somehow they are managing to prosper. I suggest to the minister that with a little technical skill and ingenuity great things could be done. There is no reason in the world why iron ore could not be brought down this short distance to Cape Breton, which is much closer to the buyers' market in New York, Montreal, indeed the whole world, instead of sending it all the way to Chicago and back again. I understand there is some problem with the sulphur content in the coal, but neither the minister nor the department could convince me that in this technological age a solution to this problem could not be found, and quickly. It needs incentive and leadership. Most of all, it needs a dedication that a solution can be found.
We should be able to make this area the steel centre of Canada, and then I dare say that the interests in Chicago and around Pittsburgh would follow this development. This is the logical place for a steel industry. The raw material is close at hand, and all we need transport to the market is the finished product, not the heavy raw material. Anyone who has been in business will understand the advantage that the maritimes have. They have coal there, iron ore close by, they have the people and the technicians. There are fantastic possibilities. This is the sort of mood I should like to see prevailing in the approach taken in any legislation.
The minister said that the production of electricity at the pithead was not a good idea, and that may be so. It may not be a good idea to bring coal out of the mines for use in producing electrical power on Cape Breton Island, which would be sent out through the grid; but there are methods today which achieve the same objective without the coal even being brought out of the mine. The coal is burned in the mine, and the heat generated is used to produce power. I believe this is being done in England today. What we need

It is not enough to say that eventually we will have to disband the coal industry, that we are not going to make use of any advantages that we have, that what we will do is to facilitate the phasing out of the industry. This is no trick. Anyone can phase out industry; the trick is to create something. Surely this is possible in our centennial year, a time when we take such great pride in our country and listen to the laurels and tributes paid our forefathers who came to this land and with their bare hands wrested the prize, which they left to us. Our forefathers did not intend us to sit idly by; they wanted us to emulate their actions, to have confidence, to know that there is a fantastic future for us, instead of taking the position that Canada is a sixth or seventh rate nation.
I fail to understand the attitude of some of the members here, Mr. Chairman. What we have not got-and this is why I decry the attitude here-is a sense of destiny and accomplishment.
I repeat, Mr. Chairman, that I am wholeheartedly in support of this resolution, but I should like to see some confidence among us here, and also some indication of what this corporation is going to do. I want to say a few words, not because we have any coal mines in my province, but because this matter is important to the economy generally of the maritime provinces. We have no coal mines in Prince Edward Island, though by devious means we have produced at least one chairman of the coal board.
I want to impress on the minister the importance of finding a solution, without reservation or hesitation, to this serious problem, and I want to ask him and the government to bring the most generous and exacting consideration to it.
The economy of any area such as Cape Breton island and eastern Nova Scotia is not an entity in itself that can be separated from the general economy of the area. When the economy of Nova Scotia is prosperous, there is an ever widening circle of economic benefit that accrues generally to the maritime provinces. When the reverse obtains we in Prince
Cape Breton Development Corporation Edward Island feel the pinch. Traditionally, when eastern Nova Scotia is prosperous we have found there an important market, chiefly for our farm and food products. When a depression or lack of employment becomes apparent in the industries of Nova Scotia, the effects, rather strikingly, are immediately and recognizably felt in the economy of Prince Edward Island.
There was a time half a century ago when the industrial prospects of eastern Nova Scotia seemed bright. That was a period of buoyancy and optimism and it had beneficial effects on the economy of the entire area. For the last 25 years we maritimers generally have been plagued by a series of industrial difficulties, first in one industry, then in another; and often these were not unrelated to each other. The failure of an industry, or the lack of vitality in an industry owing to its low profits or because it could not be viable without subventions or an artificial stimulus, had a depressing effect and lowered confidence in the whole area.
This matter is not of exclusive and direct concern to the industries in the area we talk of. What happens has a subsidiary effect on the whole economy of the maritimes. I am sorry to take time with the statement, but I want it to be understood that this is a matter in which all maritimers have a deep interest. I believe all Canadians should be deeply interested in this, and they probably are.
In the maritimes and the Atlantic provinces generally we are cursed-that is not too strong a word to use-because, to balance our economy, we have to buy for the most part manufactured goods which are manufactured chiefly in central Canada, behind protective tariff walls, and we must find markets for our own products, not generally in Canada but in foreign places. This is especially true of Newfoundland, and it is true to almost as great an extent of Nova Scotia and the other maritime provinces.
In that part of Canada we have no bargaining position vis-a-vis the rest of Canada. We cannot argue about tariffs and other arrangements which might be beneficial to large segments of our economy. We are the victims quite often of measures that are considered beneficial to Canada as a whole, or beneficial to the large economic interests. maintopic: NATIONAL DISASTERS-SUGGESTED ESTABLISHMENT OF CANADIAN FUND
NATIONAL DISASTERS-SUGGESTED ESTABLISHMENT OF CANADIAN FUND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in opening my remarks I think it is a bit unfortunate we have not got the television cameras here to televise the drama of parliament, as I have heard it called. Anyway, I must say that for years I have been convinced of the need for a national disaster fund. I remember when this idea came to my mind in embryo in 1929. I was in charge of building 20 miles of highway through a mountain pass in British Columbia. As the result of a spark coming from a locomotive climbing a steep grade I witnessed in four hours the destruction of sawmills, of homes, of farm property and of 200 million feet of timber. As a witness to the whole spectacle, I shall never forget thinking to myself that there should be some reasonable way, through law, to meet a disaster of this magnitude.
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion
In recent days, Mr. Speaker, the Fernie disaster and other disasters that have threatened as a result of forest fires and are presently threatening as the result of the flooding of some of our rivers, indicate the need is increasing for some form of national disaster fund. It was only yesterday the Minister of Industry (Mr. Drury) informed us that the Emergency Measures Act is established as a result of co-operation between the federal, provincial and municipal governments and that it can be applied on the municipal level where the resources are sufficient. Where they are not sufficient at that level they can apply to the provincial government, and where they are beyond the scope of the provincial government they can apply to the federal government. There is a logical basis for the operation of that fund, as a result of co-operation between all levels of government to meet any particular situation, whether it is in peacetime or under a wartime emergency.
It is because of my interest in this question, Mr. Speaker, that for many years I have introduced a bill entitled, "An Act to provide for the establishment of the Canada Disaster Fund." As a result of studying this bill, I find I would now call it a national disaster fund, so as not to compete with a private organization that is in the field.
I introduced this bill for the following reasons. It is intended to meet the problem of deciding at what point disaster losses are beyond the capacity of a province to deal with effectively, and the disaster essentially becomes national. The bill would set up a fund to which contributions can be made in advance by federal and provincial governments and by individuals, companies and institutions. The board of trustees would determine each year in advance, in respect of each province, the provincial financial tolerance point above which losses are of national scope. Should a disaster occur in a province the board would contribute to the province out of the fund in respect of the losses above the tolerance point.
I am not suggesting, Mr. Speaker, that this bill is perfect in all respects. It was introduced to give members an opportunity to study the question and to give the government an opportunity also to consider the importance of this matter. It was because of my interest in the subject initially, and the interest which has been stimulated as a result of my experience in this house over a period of 22 years, that I introduced the bill. It was for
June 15, 1967

Proceedings on Adjournment Motion that reason that I asked the Prime Minister the following question:
In view of the recent Fernie disaster, the possibility of disaster to the residents of Sioux Lookout and Chapleau, and other disasters, has the government given consideration to the need for a Canadian disaster fund after the fashion of the bill introduced by the member for Kootenay West, that will provide for a Canada disaster fund to which contributions can be made in advance by federal and provincial governments and by individuals, companies and institutions for assistance where the losses are considered of national scope.
I am very pleased to see the minister here this evening. I shall be interested to hear of the government's intentions with regard to the establishment of the disaster fund I have mentioned.

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Chretien (Member of the Administration):
maintopic: NATIONAL DISASTERS-SUGGESTED ESTABLISHMENT OF CANADIAN FUND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to point out to the hon. member that there is a law on the Canadian statute books entitled the Canadian Disaster Relief Fund Act. This act, passed in 1953, provides for almost the same thing for which the hon. member is asking. It sets up a corporation known as the Canadian Disaster Relief Fund, Incorporated, consisting of five members, each of whom represents one of the geographical divisions of the country. The first members of the corporation were named by the act, which provides that when a vacancy occurs in the membership of the corporation the Secretary of State may appoint a new member.
The corporation was established to manage and distribute the Canadian Disaster Relief Fund which consists of all money, property and securities received by the corporation for the purposes of the act and all income derived therefrom. No payment shall be made out of the fund except as authorized by the act. Section 6(3) of the act provides this:
The corporation may make payments out oi the fund for the purpose of meeting emergencies and needs arising in Canada from flood, fire, tempest, earthquake, pestilence or other disaster, mitigating loss and suffering caused thereby assisting in repairing damage resulting therefrom, and rehabilitating persons who have suffered injury or loss by reason thereof, when in the opinion of the corporation the implementing of such purpose is beyond the reasonable capacity of the area affected.
I think, Mr. Speaker, there are associations such as the Red Cross Society which do their best to help in these situations. In every case the government looks into the situation and does its best to improve the situation in respect of those who have suffered discomfort.

HEALTH AND WELFARE-REQUEST FOR INVESTIGATION INTO ADDITION OF ANTIBIOTICS TO LIVESTOCK FEED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday I asked a question actually of the Minister of Agriculture in the absence of the Minister of National Health and Welfare, simply because I could not decide who is responsible for the feeding of cattle in this country. In an article which appeared in the Globe and Mail of June 13 I learned that there is widespread use of large quantities of antibiotics as animal feed supplements. The danger in this regard of course is that there are remainders of small amounts of antibiotics in the meat which humans ingest every day.
In the practice of medicine we must be very careful, when we use antibiotics, that we use them in effective doses for a certain period of time until we kill the infection, rather than in small ineffective quantities, so that the bacteria do not gain the opportunity to build up resistance to the effect of the antibiotics.
e (10:10 p.m.)
I was unaware through my own ignorance, that antibiotics were used in cattle feed and that all of us were ingesting small amounts of antibiotics at all times when we ate meat. Because of the care we have to take in the practice of medicine it was a source of worry to me that possibly we are losing the effectiveness of antibiotics in that practice, because of this gradual but insidious absorption of antibiotics. I do not understand or pretend to understand the purpose of using antibiotics in cattle feeding.
There was a three day symposium held in Washington, the date of which is not given in the article, and I could not find out precisely when it was held, but according to the article Canada was one of the nations represented. It was my intention in asking the question to derive what the government's role was, what was said and what investigation is being carried out to prevent a link between the drug resistant bacteria found in man and the widespread practice of using antibiotics as a food supplement for animals whose meat we ingest.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there was a public symposium held in Washington on June 5 to June 7 on the use of drugs in animal feeds. Representatives of the food and drug directorate of the Department of National Health
June 15, 1967

and Welfare and representatives of the Department of Agriculture were in attendance.
It was evident from the proceedings of the symposium, which was attended by officers of our departments, that antibiotics added to animal feeds can result in the emergence of antibiotic resistant strains of micro-organisms. The possible impact on human health of such micro-organisms in animals is not at all clear. The Department of National Health and Welfare is continuing to keep this problem under close surveillance.

maintopic: NORTHERN AFFAIRS-FROBISHER BAY-INQUIRY AS TO HOUSING PROGRAM
NORTHERN AFFAIRS-FROBISHER BAY-INQUIRY AS TO HOUSING PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday I asked the following question to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development:
Does the department intend to carry on the intensive development program at Frobisher Bay by building this year new houses for Eskimos and government personnel?
If the Chair had not felt that the question was out of order, I would have asked the following supplementary question: Can the minister tell the house about the 1967-68 program concerning the number of units which will be built as well as their total value?
During my trips to that locality, I had the opportunity to realize the economic importance of Frobisher Bay and to consider also the sanitary needs and others for which it is urgent to make provision.
Frobisher Bay has a population of approximately 1,600 inhabitants, 1,000 of whom are Eskimos. It is the largest centre in the eastern Arctic both by its size and its large Eskimo population. It has the only international airport in the far north, and one is pleased to find that Nordair company serves this area effectively on a regular basis. It is the headquarters of a great number of government officials and other private enterprise employees who often live under deplorable conditions. Frobisher Bay is a regional centre whose administrative role is comparable to and even more important than that of centres like Churchill, Inuvik and Yellowknife. Capital investments there exceed $25 million.
Apart from the federal building which was constructed on a permanent basis, the other buildings, houses, schools, are temporary and as you all know, temporary services and quarters which are not up to Canadian standards reduce the efficiency of the workers and
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion weaken their morale. It is absolutely necessary to replace all these temporary buildings with permanent and modern constructions.
The government's construction program has been set for a five year period. In 1967, it was projected to build 30 houses for government employees and 20 for the Eskimos. This program was carried out and I want to congratulate the government for that. This does not mean, however, that all the needs have been met. Nevertheless, this was a promising start which now seems endangered for 1967-68.
This was the program for the 1967-68 period: Construction of 70 houses for government employees; construction of 100 houses for the Eskimos; construction of adjacent roads; planning for the construction of office and store buildings; preparation of plans for living quarters of 100 bachelors; preparation of plans for building a technical school.
I hardly think it is necessary to list the projects for the years to come, but I do hope that they will not be abandoned, so that the economic development of this area may be pursued satisfactorily.
However, I note that vote No. 25 of the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development in the estimates for 1967-68 provides no money for part of the 1967-68 program, particularly for the following items, according to the replies given by the minister to the member for the Northwest Territories (Mr. Orange) at the beginning of June: No money to continue the program to build 70 houses for government employees; no money to prepare plans for the construction of office and store buildings; no money for the preparation of plans to build living quarters for 100 bachelors.
Due to the fact that Frobisher Bay has no basic resources and is entirely dependent on the government for its existence, this attitude by the department is causing a feeling of frustration and instability among the population and, consequently, is reducing its productivity and legitimate aspirations.
I hope that the government will not only continue the program submitted to and accepted by Treasury Board but that it will step it up and improve it.
